# Wattever

> LLM endpoint throughput and deterministic task-accuracy benchmarking with optional local telemetry, public model configuration identities and shareable audit JSON. The Python helper supports managed LM Studio or externally managed streaming Chat Completions. Hosted browser timing uses a separate protocol; its capability catalog is read-only.

## Core docs

- [Overview](README.md): quick start and project scope.
- [Documentation index](docs/README.md): full guide map.
- [Browser mode](docs/browser.md): hosted connection, measurement and storage limits.
- [Sharing results](docs/sharing-results.md): shared catalog, contributions and continuing helper sessions.

- [RTX 5060 Ti storage comparison](docs/5060-ti-storage-comparison.md): recorded Strata SATA/NVMe timings, repeats, speedups and hardware conditions.
- [RTX 5070 Ti hardware and storage follow-up](docs/5070-ti-hardware-follow-up.md): 144 completed paired storage observations, prefill/decode aggregates, actual drafting evidence, transfer measurements and the pending active-channel report.

- [PNY RTX 5070 Ti plus ASUS RTX 5060 Ti](docs/5070-plus-5060-comparison.md): matched and supplemental LM Studio measurements, per-card/combined energy, transfer/compute probes, connection diagnostics and Strata coverage status.
- [Multi-GPU communication and placement study](docs/dual-gpu-communication-and-placement.md): communication paths, transfer measurements, GPU execution strategies, profiling evidence and diagnostic protocol boundaries.
- [Two RTX 5070 Ti cards](docs/two-5070-ti-comparison.md): 180 normal cases, matched single/mixed-card throughput and energy, native drafting and temperatures; separate three-repeat Flash expert-RAM tables at 40,960 and 131,072 context.
- [vLLM on two RTX 5070 Ti cards](docs/vllm-two-5070-ti.md): NVFP4 Qwen3.8-27B in vLLM versus LM Studio Q4_K_M, context-pool memory settings, prefix reuse, tensor versus pipeline parallelism and energy.
- [Two RTX 5070 Ti placement strategies](docs/two-5070-ti-placement.md): measured communication paths, standalone prefill/decode, independent instances, energy and profiling limits.
- [Capability evaluation](docs/capabilities.md): visual score/coverage dashboard, question-by-repeat evidence explorer, pinned Core/GSM8K/ARC/MMLU-Pro suites and paired-comparison limits.
- [Flash-Next task accuracy](docs/flash-next-quality.md): UD-IQ4_XS and IQ3_S on matched public-question samples, audit answers, coverage and generation conditions on two RTX 5070 Ti cards.
- [Experiment checkpoint](docs/experiment-status.md): completed dual-5070 performance, communication and quality measurements; explicit GLM download/preparation status without inference claims.
- [Architecture](docs/architecture.md): components and boundaries.
- [Local inference upgrades](docs/local-inference-upgrades.md): ten ranked upgrade routes for the dual-5070 Ti machine, supported RAM/platform limits and purchasing evidence.

## README.md

Canonical source: [README.md](README.md)

# Wattever

Wattever benchmarks LLM endpoints across prompt sizes, models and simultaneous query counts, and compares successes and failures in a browser UI. Connect the local Python helper or hosted browser to an OpenAI-compatible streaming Chat Completions endpoint, including Strata, llama.cpp and LM Studio. The helper also offers managed LM Studio model loading and optional local GPU power measurements. Wattever uses Python 3.9+, the Python standard library and local JavaScript without a package installation or CDN.

The interface has five tabs: **System** for hardware inventory and live readings, **Benchmarks** for configuring and running workloads, **Results** for analysis, **Capabilities** for task evaluations, and **Share** for result exchange. System monitoring is independent of the inference connection in the local helper. See [sharing results](docs/sharing-results.md) for JSON and GitHub contributions.

## Browser quick start

Open [Wattever on GitHub Pages](https://lpalbou.github.io/Wattever/), start an OpenAI-compatible server, enable its CORS support, and use **Connect** to select models and run tests. Browser and server permissions can affect access to a local endpoint. See [Browser mode](docs/browser.md) for settings, storage, privacy and measurement limits.

## Full local helper quick start

1. Start your inference engine and load a model. For managed LM Studio operation, install LM Studio, download models and run `lms bootstrap` once. Other endpoints do not need LM Studio.
2. Download and extract the [Wattever 2.6.1 source archive](https://github.com/lpalbou/Wattever/releases/download/v2.6.1/Wattever-2.6.1.zip), or clone the repository. Use the matching documentation and source version.
3. On Windows run `Wattever.bat`; on macOS run `Wattever.command`; on Linux run `sh Wattever.sh`. Alternatively run `python -m wattever.server` from the repository.
4. Open the displayed local URL. On **Benchmarks**, choose **OpenAI-compatible endpoint**, enter your API base URL and use **Connect**. Wattever identifies the endpoint where evidence is available and supplies its display name automatically; no manual label or ID is required. Enter a model ID manually if discovery is unavailable. Select each desired prompt size and concurrent query count independently, then start. Leave the server running until the benchmark finishes.

See [Getting started](docs/getting-started.md) for both provider modes and [Measurements and sessions](docs/measurements.md) for interpretation. The external inference engine controls model loading, quantization, context, KV cache, GPU placement and speculative decoding. With Strata Control, start the server and load the model there; connecting Wattever does not start or switch Strata models. Generic endpoint power measurements require an explicit assertion that inference runs on the benchmark computer; remote inference power remains unavailable.

**Results** has three views in order. **Overview** describes the selected system and, for each model, its peak prefill and decode speed, how both change as prompts grow, the longest prompt that completed, and what happens with concurrent queries; any figure opens its graph. **Graphs & comparisons** is driven by a control panel of toggle buttons: tick any metrics (each gets its own chart), choose whether to plot against prompt length or concurrent queries, tick the query counts or prompt lengths to draw as separate lines, tick models, and colour the curves by model or by benchmark. Hover a chart to compare every line at that point. **Tables & CSV** exposes numerical results and raw repeats. See [Concurrency comparisons](docs/concurrency.md).

The local helper supports **Add / rerun tests** for managed LM Studio and reconnected external endpoints. One JSON file stores each benchmark. Review it before publication; see [results guidance](results/README.md).

Benchmarks of one machine merge into one: tick them in Results and choose **Merge into one…**. Wattever recognizes the machine, including for endpoint benchmarks saved as remote, explains what cannot join, and can undo the merge. Consolidation preserves engine/session settings and exact measurement rows. Conflicting known GPU board identities remain separate even when the GPU chip name matches; legacy unknown board metadata stays unknown.

The **System** tab's collapsed **This machine** header shows CPU, GPU, RAM and per-card VRAM. Expand it for grouped compute, storage, transfer and platform cards; full names and probe methods stay accessible. Compatible saved transfer captures retain their original date and are labeled **Saved capture**.

System also provides colored utilization and memory gauges with sparklines and a history explorer. The helper records the machine every second for as long as it runs, whether or not System is open, and keeps the last 24 hours on this computer in the gitignored `results/.telemetry/`, so you can check what happened at a given time. Select metrics or a preset, choose a window from 1 minute to 24 hours, step to an earlier interval or go to a date and time, overlay compatible units, pause history, or inspect samples with the pointer or time slider. Axes and readouts show local clock times, with the date when it is not today. Long windows average the 1-second readings and the readout adds the peak. Relative overlay scales each metric to its own visible peak; it compares trends rather than physical magnitudes. Sampling gaps and times when the helper was not running remain empty. The browser-only site requires the local helper for sensors.

GPU, memory, storage and engine-setting badges summarize recorded conditions. Storage types use **HDD**, **SSD** and **NVMe**; unknown types stay unclassified. If an experiment contains alternative storage observations, **Compare recorded storage** selects the measured variants. Installed drives and storage probes alone do not create inference variants. See the [RTX 5060 Ti Strata comparison](docs/5060-ti-storage-comparison.md) for the measured gains and conditions.

The [two RTX 5070 Ti comparison](docs/two-5070-ti-comparison.md) records 180 normal cases across LM Studio and native Strata, with matched throughput, energy, drafting and per-card thermal observations.

The [vLLM on two RTX 5070 Ti cards](docs/vllm-two-5070-ti.md) study serves NVIDIA's NVFP4 Qwen3.8-27B with vLLM against LM Studio, with the memory settings for a 188,832-token context pool, prefix reuse, tensor versus pipeline parallelism and energy per batch.

The separate [prefill scheduling study](docs/prefill-scheduling-and-concurrency.md) measures fair-admission tradeoffs, independent GPU replicas and Q8-cache context capacity, with raw diagnostic timing/power evidence and reproducible configurations.

The [GLM-5.3-Flash study](docs/glm53-flash-comparison.md) reports preliminary Maya-XS measurements from the existing NVMe, actual pinned expert memory and descriptive Flash-Next comparisons. Optimization and quality results remain separate.

The [multi-GPU communication and placement study](docs/dual-gpu-communication-and-placement.md) examines execution strategies with separate diagnostic protocols. Transfer microbenchmarks and profiled inference captures stay separate from the normal benchmark library. Study tools have their own platform and dependency requirements.

The hosted Results view also includes a shared catalog that you can browse without connecting a model provider. See [sharing results](docs/sharing-results.md) to contribute your benchmark or add missing tests later.

## Capability tests and live telemetry

The helper's **Capabilities** tab runs original Core tasks and pinned GSM8K, ARC-Challenge and MMLU-Pro test questions. MMLU-Pro offers its full 12,032-question split or a fixed 64-question sample balanced across 14 subjects. Choose a deterministic subset or the full suite and compare auditable rule-scored answers. These are zero-shot chat adaptations, separate from official leaderboard scores and intelligence rankings. Requested reasoning, reported MTP/quantization and unknown effective settings remain distinct in public model/endpoint configuration fingerprints. See [capability evaluation](docs/capabilities.md) for scoring, dataset licenses and uncertainty.

The [Flash-Next accuracy collection](docs/flash-next-quality.md) compares UD-IQ4_XS and IQ3_S on the same ARC64, GSM64 and MMLU-Pro64 samples, with inspectable answers and complete question coverage, separately from throughput measurements.

The [experiment checkpoint](docs/experiment-status.md) brings together the completed dual-5070 results and distinguishes them from GLM-5.3-Flash preparation, which has no inference measurements yet.

Its visual dashboard combines strict pass rate, correct/planned and coverage tiles with category bars, an outcome ring and repeat comparisons. Select a chart to filter the paginated question-by-repeat matrix, then open a cell to inspect the question, expected output, model response and rule explanation. Matching evaluation protocols support paired comparisons that exclude unscored requests. A format mismatch or request error is shown distinctly from a passed answer; inspect the evidence before drawing conclusions about reasoning.

Local runs can display CPU/GPU utilization, RAM/VRAM usage, available temperatures, GPU clocks and power. On supported NVIDIA systems, measurements cover all detected cards with individual readings and combined GPU board power. Concurrent requests share one group energy window, so overlapping request energy is not added together. CPU/system power estimates remain labeled separately from measured GPU power; they are not wall-meter readings.

Saved telemetry includes a bounded recent history and whole-run observed means/peaks/coverage; early/late changes are observations, not a throttling diagnosis. Results charts separate selected metrics into individual graphs. The hosted site can browse/export/compare shared capability results; launching tests and validating capability imports require the helper.

Register and use the [Wattever agent skill](skills/wattever/SKILL.md) to operate the local API. Copy `skills/wattever/` from the version you use into your agent's skills directory.

## docs/getting-started.md

Canonical source: [docs/getting-started.md](docs/getting-started.md)

# Getting started

For hosted use without installing Wattever, see [Browser mode](docs/browser.md). The instructions below cover the full local helper.

Install Python 3.9 or newer. Wattever does not need Python packages or a JavaScript build. Choose a provider mode:

- **OpenAI-compatible endpoint:** start an inference engine such as Strata, llama.cpp or LM Studio and load your model there. Wattever needs streaming Chat Completions; model discovery is optional. Other OpenAI API surfaces are not required or implemented by this integration.
- **LM Studio (managed):** install [LM Studio](https://lmstudio.ai/), download models and run `lms bootstrap`. Wattever can load/unload models and schedule context and MTP settings through its CLI. The API defaults to `http://127.0.0.1:1234`; `LMS_BASE_URL` changes that managed connection. Explicit configured URLs and saved measurements keep their original addresses and timing provenance.

Download and extract the [Wattever 2.6.1 source archive](https://github.com/lpalbou/Wattever/releases/download/v2.6.1/Wattever-2.6.1.zip), or clone the repository. Use documentation matching that source version. Start `Wattever.bat` on Windows, `Wattever.command` on macOS, or `sh Wattever.sh` on Linux. You can also run `python -m wattever.server` in the extracted folder or repository. The server listens on loopback and prints its URL; keep its window open. `GPU_BENCH_PORT` sets the starting port (default 8713); `GPU_BENCH_NO_BROWSER=1` suppresses automatic browser opening.

On **Benchmarks**, choose your provider. For a generic endpoint, enter your engine's API base URL, such as `http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1` (a root URL also works), and, under **Connection options**, its API key if it needs one. The key is sent only to that endpoint and is never saved, so enter it again after reloading the page. Click **Connect**. Wattever supplies a display name and an opaque route identity automatically; no label or ID is required. Model discovery lists the IDs exposed by the connected endpoint. If the provider does not expose `/models`, supply its exact served model ID manually. The Python helper connects directly, so browser CORS permission is only needed in hosted browser mode.

Endpoint names come from recognized public cloud hosts or explicit service metadata when available. Local/private metadata probes are bounded, read-only requests; Wattever does not identify software from a port number or model name. If the software cannot be established, it uses an honest **Local endpoint**, **Private endpoint** or **Remote endpoint** fallback. An optional advanced **Display name** override is the only naming field you need to edit. Detected route location does not establish where inference runs; the local-inference confirmation remains a separate assertion.

Select models, prompt sizes, query counts and repeats. Configure quantization, context allocation, KV cache, placement and MTP in the external engine. **Requested reasoning** defaults to **None** in the UI and sends `reasoning_effort`; choose **Provider default** to omit it. Unsupported values fail visibly, and accepted requests do not verify effective behavior. Reproducibility fields and reported MTP/reasoning record operator knowledge; they do not change the engine. A canonical model ID can identify a checkpoint behind a served alias. To add or repair models inside an existing GPU benchmark, reconnect its endpoint and choose **Add / rerun tests** in Results. External model loading stays under the engine's control. LM Studio also supports automatic load/unload and separate-file resume.

With Strata Control, start the Strata server and load your chosen model in that application before connecting. Wattever does not start, switch or restore Strata models. Multiple detected GPUs do not establish that a model uses every card: supported placement, tensor parallelism and KV-cache modes depend on the serving engine and model architecture. Record the effective settings reported by the backend; a requested or accepted mode alone is not proof of its execution.

Hardware discovery describes the benchmark client. Leave **Inference runs on this computer** unchecked for remote or uncertain deployments. Checking it explicitly attributes local sensors to inference; it does not verify the server's hardware. Telemetry does not select execution placement. On supported NVIDIA systems, the helper records every detected card's power, utilization, VRAM, clocks and available temperature, together with combined GPU board power. Missing readings remain unavailable. Concurrent workloads use one group energy window, retaining per-card contributions without adding overlapping request energy. CPU/system estimates are separate from measured GPU power and do not replace a wall meter. Record placement and other relevant settings, and close competing workloads for comparisons. The macOS launcher offers optional authorization for `powermetrics`; throughput measurements work without it.

Use **Results** to select benchmarks: click a name to open one, tick several to compare machines. **Overview** shows the system and each model's peak speeds, trends and limits. In **Graphs & comparisons**, tick the metrics, models and query counts to draw; every choice is a visible toggle. Prompt length is the default horizontal axis, and **Concurrent queries** is offered when more than one query count was recorded. Colour the curves by model or by benchmark. **Tables & CSV** comes last and retains exact measurements, raw repeats and downloads. See [measurements](docs/measurements.md) before comparing and [troubleshooting](docs/troubleshooting.md) if setup fails. Return to [overview](README.md); see [API](docs/api.md) for integration.

Benchmarks measured on one machine, such as an LM Studio run and a Strata run, can become one benchmark so engines compare side by side. Tick them and choose **Merge into one…**, or use the **Same machine** suggestion the library shows when it recognizes such a group. The dialog says which benchmarks can join and why another cannot, and asks you to confirm **Inference ran on this machine** for an endpoint benchmark that was saved as remote. A test measured more than once keeps its completed, most recent measurement; the others stay in the benchmark's history. The originals move to the local archive, and **Undo merge** on the merged benchmark brings them back unchanged, as long as no tests were added to or removed from it since.

Keep manufacturer/model/memory board annotations when comparing cards with the same GPU chip. Consolidation rejects conflicting known board identities or known variants while retaining compatibility with legacy unknown metadata; it preserves the original measurement rows and source evidence.

For controlled GPU transfer and placement experiments, see the [multi-GPU engineering study](docs/dual-gpu-communication-and-placement.md). Its diagnostic captures, profiling overhead and study tools have separate protocols and requirements; they are not added to normal benchmark aggregates.

Use **Capabilities** for task accuracy after connecting in **Benchmarks**. Select a model, suite and question count, review the answer budget and timeout, then start. Full suites can be lengthy; subsets record their exact seeded selection. Capability tests and validated imports require the helper. The hosted site supports their shared result library/export/comparison. See [capability evaluation](docs/capabilities.md).

After updating Python or UI files, restart the helper and reload its page to use the complete build. The launcher identifies builds with `/api/version` `build_id`, reuses the same build, and can replace an identified idle older build even when the release version is unchanged. Active speed or capability runs are preserved. Use the printed helper URL; its port is separate from your model server's port, and restarting Wattever does not require stopping the inference engine.

After a timeout or cancellation, the helper remains busy while outstanding request workers are alive. Its status explains that it is waiting; new speed and capability runs become available when those workers exit. An external server may still be computing after a client request ends, so check its state before restarting a comparison.

---

## docs/browser.md

Canonical source: [docs/browser.md](docs/browser.md)

# Browser mode

Open [Wattever on GitHub Pages](https://lpalbou.github.io/Wattever/) to run a quick benchmark without installing Wattever. Start LM Studio or another OpenAI-compatible server with models available. Enter its endpoint (the default is `http://localhost:1234/v1`) and select **Connect**; Wattever does not request the model list until you connect. Choose models and workloads, start the benchmark, and keep the page open until it finishes.

The provider must permit cross-origin requests. LM Studio has an Enable CORS switch in its [server settings](https://lmstudio.ai/docs/developer/core/server/settings). Browsers may also require local-network permission, and HTTPS-to-localhost behavior depends on the browser and its security settings; see [Microsoft Edge local network access](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/deployedge/ms-edge-local-network-access). Wattever connects directly from the browser: it has no hosted proxy and does not use helper credentials. If the endpoint needs an API key, enter it in the page; the key stays in memory and the input clears after connecting. It is not saved in result files or browser storage.

Endpoint names and route IDs are automatic. Recognized official cloud hosts or explicit service metadata can identify the service; otherwise a Local/Private/Remote endpoint fallback is used. No manual label or ID is required, and an advanced **Display name** override is optional. Canonical known public API routes use stable public provider IDs; other routes, including custom cloud paths, use a private URL-to-random-ID mapping in browser local storage. That mapping is excluded from exports; clearing storage can regenerate its IDs. Detection describes the route/provider, not verified inference hardware or backend weights.

Chrome versions with separate network permissions may call localhost access **Apps on device** or **Loopback network**. Allow the permission for the Wattever site when you connect. The permission is distinct from access to other devices on your LAN; see [Chrome local network guidance](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/security/local-network-access.md).

GPU, CPU, RAM and VRAM fields are optional user-supplied descriptions, not hardware discovery. Browser mode cannot measure GPU power or VRAM use, load/unload models, choose placement, allocate context, control MTP, resume a session or extend the same file. It can request standard reasoning effort, temperature and the supported token-limit field; the engine's effective behavior remains unverified. Unsupported request values fail visibly. Configure model execution in the provider. Use the [local helper](docs/getting-started.md) for detected client hardware and optional local telemetry; its managed LM Studio provider additionally supports lifecycle/context controls and same-file extension.

New browser results record `measurement_mode: browser`, `browser_schema_version: 2` and protocol `browser-2`, with bundled corpus identity and a SHA-256 hash when available. Timing includes network/browser overhead and is not directly comparable to helper protocols. Exact provider usage is required for token throughput; missing counts remain unavailable, with no character/chunk token estimate. Reasoning usage and observed output boundaries are recorded: reported unstreamed reasoning is excluded from decode, ambiguous hidden reasoning or a single output event leaves decode unavailable. Prompt tokens/client TTFT remains a proxy including possible hidden work, not isolated engine compute. Public model configuration fingerprints distinguish requested/reported/unknown settings without storing connection URLs. Historical `browser-1` files remain readable and may include estimated throughput; compare their protocol/provenance separately.

Results are stored in browser storage and can be downloaded or imported as JSON. Storage can be cleared or unavailable; if a storage warning appears, download the in-memory results before closing the page. Closing or reloading the page stops the browser benchmark, and a previously running result is shown as interrupted. On timeout the browser aborts its requests and stops the run, but cannot verify that the provider stopped inference or unload its model. Check the provider before starting another workload. Helper benchmarks instead continue in the local server when the page closes; see [measurements and sessions](docs/measurements.md).

Results also shows a read-only shared catalog without requiring an endpoint connection. Hiding a shared result affects only this browser. See [sharing results](docs/sharing-results.md) to contribute a benchmark.

## Shared-results data boundary

The hosted site opens the shared Results library by default. Browsing it reads only the same-origin GitHub Pages catalog and benchmark JSON; it does not query desktop helper APIs or local files. Shared records identify their GitHub source. The published JSON omits host-local diagnostic text and paths while preserving measurements, failure classifications, hardware descriptions, settings and session provenance. It is a public projection of the repository record.

If the browser data client fails to load, the hosted site reports that failure rather than falling back to desktop APIs. Model-server access belongs to the optional Run workflow and starts only after an explicit Connect action.

The **Capabilities** library reads same-origin shared capability files, verifies their catalog SHA-256 and supports export/comparison. Dataset/score validation occurs during publication with the helper's deterministic re-scoring and fingerprint checks. The hosted page cannot launch capability tests or import unvalidated capability files; use the helper for those actions. Throughput JSON import remains available in browser Results. See [capability evaluation](docs/capabilities.md).

---

## docs/sharing-results.md

Canonical source: [docs/sharing-results.md](docs/sharing-results.md)

# Sharing and continuing benchmark results

The hosted Results view includes a shared catalog built from benchmark JSON files in this repository, alongside results stored in your browser. You can browse shared results without connecting a model provider or entering an API key. Shared entries are read-only; deleting one in the hosted view hides it in that browser and does not delete it from GitHub. Local browser results can be renamed and deleted locally.

Select benchmarks in Results or evaluations in Capabilities, then use **Share** to download individual `<id>.json` files or export a bundle. Split bundles into individual files before contributing. Share provides GitHub upload and pull-request links for both result types; submit reviewed files through GitHub. Benchmark JSON can also be downloaded from Results; browser benchmark JSON import is available in the Results library. Capability imports require the local helper.

## Contribute a benchmark

1. Run a benchmark using the [full helper](docs/getting-started.md) or [browser mode](docs/browser.md). Partial sessions and failures are useful contributions too.
2. In Results, download the benchmark's **JSON**. Review hardware information and all free text, including notes, model names, labels, reproduction fields and compute sources. Public outputs exclude endpoint URLs, credentials and credential environment-variable names; that filtering cannot decide whether your annotations are confidential. Browser results identify their separate client-timed protocol; helper results include sensor/session settings.
3. Sign in to GitHub and open [upload files to results/runs](https://github.com/lpalbou/Wattever/upload/main/results/runs). Upload the single JSON file, named after its `id` with a `.json` extension. If you do not have write access, follow GitHub's fork prompt and propose the change from your fork.
4. Open the proposed pull request. The repository's validation checks run on the contribution. Once merged and the site deployment completes, the shared catalog updates automatically.

For a command-line contribution, fork and clone the repository, create a branch, and copy the single result file to `results/runs/`. Run `python tools/validate_results.py results/runs/<id>.json`, then `git add results/runs/<id>.json`, commit, push your branch and open a pull request. Stage the specific result file so unrelated local files and deletions are excluded.

For a linked machine comparison, contribute every member listed in `comparison_group.run_ids`, including its root run. **Open machine benchmark** then selects the available members together in Results. The files retain separate engines, settings and sessions; a group does not turn externally queued requests into parallel backend execution. Use clear labels and optional public `tags` for the GPU, engine, model, quantization and technique; tags appear with the run's scientific metadata. Review notes and recorded runtime observations alongside requested/reported/effective settings. See [machine comparison linking](docs/api.md).

To keep one entry per machine configuration, merge its benchmarks before contributing: tick them in Results and choose **Merge into one…**, or use the helper's [consolidation route](docs/api.md). Publish the resulting single JSON file and remove the superseded source entries from the active catalog. Engine-specific results, settings and provenance remain inside the benchmark's sessions, `engine_groups` and source metadata. Consolidation preserves measurement rows and does not change the backend's concurrency behavior.

## Open a model comparison

Use `?compare=<benchmark-id>,<benchmark-id>#results` on a source-checkout helper or the hosted site to open two to eight catalog entries together. The link selects their shared model IDs, one concurrent client, both speculative-decoding modes, and separate prefill/decode charts for each model. Choose other metrics or query counts in Results. All referenced benchmark IDs must exist in that catalog; a link containing unknown IDs is ignored without fetching arbitrary resources.

For example, [compare the single and dual RTX 5070 Ti configurations](https://lpalbou.github.io/Wattever/?compare=20261102-041639_rtx-5070-ti_6b6060174b,20261103-100532_rtx-5070-ti_0a91ddc850#results). Shared model IDs do not establish identical weights or settings: review quantization, engine, reasoning, MTP, token counts and timing definitions. The [dual-card report](docs/two-5070-ti-comparison.md) covers 180 attempted normal cases, with 179 successes and one native Qwen35 timeout, and 13 shared model IDs against the single-PNY benchmark. Standalone diagnostics and profiled captures remain separate. Historical LM Studio localhost timings and explicit-IPv4 timings retain their observations, without a guessed latency correction.

Selected primary conditions remain selected when consolidation creates engine-specific views. Explicitly cleared selections and engine or storage subsets retain their choices. Partial experiment metadata identifies planned cases that have no observations.

## Add missing tests later

Same-file additions and repairs support managed LM Studio and generic helper endpoints. Reconnect the matching external endpoint in Benchmarks before using Results; connection details are not stored in public files, and model loading stays with the engine operator. Browser experiments require a new run. Separate-file resume is managed-only.

A benchmark does not need every planned case before you contribute it. To complete or extend a helper benchmark later, download its JSON and put it in the local helper's `results/runs/` directory using its `id` as the filename. Connect its engine in Benchmarks. In Results select it and choose **Add / rerun tests**. Existing models are preselected; select the models, sizes and query counts you want, review the preview, and choose **Add missing tests**. Existing terminal cases are preserved. Increase **Total repeats per test** to append repeats. To replace one specific measurement, choose its entry in **Tests to update**; previous attempts remain in history. Select **Retry failed tests** explicitly if you also want to retry failures and skipped cases.

The helper checks hardware, selected GPU/driver and corpus for compatibility. Managed additions also check LM Studio version; external repairs require the saved endpoint identity and a fresh connection. Start a separate benchmark when required conditions differ or cannot be verified. The same file records the added session and the helper saves a backup before modifying it. To update a contribution, submit the updated file with the same ID in a pull request; the saved cases travel with it. Do not manually edit measurements or replace failures with zeroes.

Browser mode can import and display JSON but cannot continue an existing benchmark. Its provider controls model execution and context. See [measurements and sessions](docs/measurements.md) for retry, replacement and comparison rules.

## Reproducibility metadata

Hardware inventory describes the benchmark client. For remote inference, the result retains client inventory separately and does not claim it describes the server. Include public engine/version, model revision, quantization, actual context/KV settings, MTP draft count and runtime placement when known. Optional reproduction fields are marked `user_reported`; they do not configure the engine.

Only add compute claims with a source, arithmetic precision, execution path, dense/sparse distinction and peak/measured/estimate classification. INT precision uses TOPS; floating precision uses TFLOP/s. A claim is not a Wattever measurement. PCIe encoding ceilings are not measured DMA bandwidth, and idle link state can differ from loaded state. Compare client timings, provider timings and cache usage using their separate provenance; unknown cache usage is not zero. See [measurement definitions](docs/measurements.md).

## Capability results

Use **Capabilities → Export JSON** for one or more capability runs. These use `benchmark_kind: capability`, their own schema 1 and `results/capabilities/<id>.json`; keep throughput files in `results/runs/`. A `capability_runs` bundle is convenient for helper import/export; contribute individual run files under their IDs. The hosted catalog supports browsing/export/comparison; tests and validated imports require the helper. The hosted site does not write to GitHub.

Review generated visible answers, prompts, expected answers and source citations, as well as labels/notes and reported settings. Public audit material preserves exact content for dataset/protocol fingerprints and independent rescoring. Privacy-redacted responses are marked and cannot be re-imported as full, independently scored audit answers. Keep a reviewed original if needed.

Import re-scores answers and checks configuration/suite/protocol/subset fingerprints. These establish consistency, not authentication or proof that a model ran. Compare matching evaluation keys with scored/error/truncation counts and requested/reported/unknown effective settings. Automatically resolved opaque IDs and display names identify routes without sharing or hashing connection URLs. Keep the private helper/browser URL-to-ID registry out of contributions. See [capability evaluation](docs/capabilities.md).

---

## docs/measurements.md

Canonical source: [docs/measurements.md](docs/measurements.md)

﻿# Measurements and sessions

The local helper supports managed LM Studio and generic OpenAI-compatible endpoints. Hosted browser mode uses a separate `browser-2` protocol; historical `browser-1` files remain readable. Browser/helper timings and historical estimates are not directly interchangeable. See [Browser mode](docs/browser.md).

## Throughput and timing

A case combines a model, technique, prompt size, simultaneous query count and repeat. Successful, failed and skipped cases are recorded; inability to load or fit a workload is useful capacity information. The library reports successful, failed, skipped and cancelled counts separately; an unattempted skipped repeat is not counted as a measured failure. Managed LM Studio can schedule Standard/MTP modes when a supported bundled MTP head exists, and disables reasoning by default. Generic endpoint technique, reasoning, context allocation, KV cache and quantization are controlled by the inference engine. Their effective state is unknown unless documented separately by the operator; a scheduler technique label does not prove the server's MTP state.

When a provider supplies per-request `draft_n` and `draft_n_accepted` timing
counters, Wattever retains validated nonnegative integer counts. Missing
counters remain unknown. Acceptance cannot exceed the offered count; requested
drafting and observed proposals remain separate evidence.

For one request, client timings use a monotonic clock with these boundaries:

| Metric | Boundary / calculation |
|---|---|
| `ttft_s` | Request start to first observed nonempty content or reasoning output. This is the client prefill proxy; queueing and network time are included. |
| `decode_s` | First observed nonempty output to **last observed nonempty output**. Prefill/TTFT and trailing usage, finish markers or EOF delivery are excluded. |
| `response_tail_s` | Last observed output to completed stream delivery. This is separate from generation time. |
| `wall_s` | Request start through completed response delivery, including all phases and transport tail. |
| `prefill_tps` | Prompt tokens divided by client prefill-proxy time. |
| `decode_tps` | Scoped decode tokens divided by decode time; **never** divided by end-to-end wall time. |
| `group_output_tps` | Total completion tokens divided by end-to-end wall time; this is a separately labeled end-to-end rate. |

A single output event has no observed interval between output events, so decode throughput is unavailable. Delaying usage or EOF packets must not lengthen decode time. Backend-reported engine counters remain in `reported_timings` and are not substituted for client timings. Client TTFT does not isolate the instant an engine receives or starts processing a prompt; pure engine prefill requires backend evidence.

For concurrent requests, retain each request's start offset from the common batch clock. Total decode throughput is the sum of scoped `decode_token_count` values divided by the **union** of successful requests' post-first-token decode intervals. Overlapping intervals count once; gaps in which no request is decoding are excluded. A sum of request rates can overstate serialized work, and whole-batch wall time wrongly includes prefill. The prefill proxy similarly uses the union of request-start-to-first-output intervals. These observed proxy intervals can include queueing and another stream's decoding; they are not isolated engine compute intervals. Concurrent phase unions can overlap, so their durations must not be added to reconstruct batch wall time.

Concurrent `wall_s` runs from batch dispatch through the final request's completion. The TTFT shown per request is its median across requests, distinct from the total prefill-proxy interval. Successful complete groups contribute to comparison charts; failed and incomplete groups retain inspectable partial evidence without being treated as successful throughput. Missing offsets, durations or scoped counts leave derived phase rates unavailable.

Server token usage supplies the output numerator. Hidden reasoning reported by the server is excluded from the scoped decode count when it was not streamed; unknown hidden work remains explicitly uncertain. No token rate is inferred by counting characters or stream chunks. The conventional first-token correction subtracts one token from scoped usage. Because the first received chunk can contain several tokens, its exact token boundary is unknown; `timing_scope.decode_count_estimated_boundary` records that approximation and decode plots/tables mark it. Live progress can report **chunks/s**, explicitly separate from final tokens/s.

`timing_scope` records output kinds, reasoning usage provenance, first-chunk uncertainty and the decode end boundary. New records identify the last observed output boundary. Historical records can contain first-output-to-EOF durations; without a recorded last-output timestamp their transport tail cannot be recovered. Those derived decode values remain marked approximate. Historical raw observations are preserved rather than silently rewritten. Exported derived fields retain recorded values and sources for audit.

Results exposes total decode throughput, median per-request decode, decode time, client-prefill-proxy time, and end-to-end output throughput as separate metrics. Axis switches preserve a metric's meaning or explicitly disable an unsupported combination. CSV includes scoped counts, request timing evidence and provenance. GPU decode energy covers the same first-to-last-output window as decode throughput. Whole-case GPU energy uses its independently sampled full-request window; it is not fabricated by adding incomplete or differently bounded phase windows. Provider-reported prompt/decode counters stay separate.

## Context and workload

For managed LM Studio, the default per-test allocation reserves prompt tokens, output budget, 512 tokens of headroom and a 5% prompt safety margin, subject to the model's per-request maximum. Shared KV allocation multiplies per-request capacity by concurrency. The per-test policy reloads for each context/concurrency allocation; the optional fixed policy uses the largest planned allocation per model and MTP mode, reducing reloads while changing memory conditions. Generic endpoint context estimates describe client workload planning only; configure the real context/KV allocation in the engine. More concurrency consumes more memory; large contexts can fail to fit.

In Benchmarks and Add / rerun tests, select each prompt size and concurrent query count independently; selecting a larger value does not add smaller values. The selected sizes and query counts form the workload combinations. Prompt presets are 512, 5k, 10k, 20k, 40k, 80k, 100k, 120k, 150k, 200k and 260k tokens; concurrency presets are 1 through 10, 15, 20, 30, 40, 50, 75 and 100. Compare cases at matching dimensions, output budget and repeat count. Close competing workloads and record relevant clock/power settings and runtime placement.

## Hardware, power and provenance

NVIDIA telemetry uses one `nvidia-smi` process to sample every detected NVIDIA card. New runs retain each card's board power, utilization, used/capacity VRAM, temperature and SM clock, plus combined GPU totals. Power and physical VRAM usage are summed at the same monitor timestamps; utilization is an unweighted mean, temperature is the maximum reported value, and separate clocks remain per card. Summed physical VRAM does not imply pooled allocations. Missing/stale readings make the corresponding complete aggregate unavailable. macOS may use `powermetrics` for GPU and CPU rails with permission; these have different boundaries. Whole-system power remains an estimate: combined GPU power plus CPU and other-system estimates, counted once. Primary GPU selection identifies the benchmark; it does not restrict monitoring or select inference placement. Generic endpoint power is unavailable unless `endpoint_inference_local: true` explicitly asserts that inference runs on the benchmark client. An externally loaded model prevents a verified unloaded-model idle baseline. Historical selected-card measurements retain their original scope and are never reconstructed as all-card totals.

Hardware inventory is a best-effort, read-only snapshot of the benchmark client, not verified remote server hardware. Additive `metadata_schema_version: 1` metadata accompanies result `schema_version: 2`; historical files remain readable. Available fields include CPU/socket/core counts, RAM modules and reported clocks, GPU VRAM/driver, and current/max-reported PCIe generation and width. DIMM count does not establish active channels. PCIe snapshots can downshift while idle; reported maxima may reflect platform limits. `link_encoding_ceiling_bytes_per_second` is a derived one-direction ceiling after encoding only, excluding packet/system overhead. It is neither a measured DMA rate nor device-memory bandwidth. Unmeasured bandwidth remains null.

Memory topology is collected automatically without installing utilities. Windows reads SMBIOS through `GetSystemFirmwareTable`: populated Type 37 channel records take precedence; explicit Type 17 channel/slot labels provide a separately labeled firmware-layout inference. Linux uses populated EDAC channel locations where available. Other or incomplete reports remain unavailable. Raw firmware identifiers and slot labels are not retained. `memory.channel_topology` records the source, method, timestamp, populated channel count and independently detected active count, if supplied. **Populated channels do not prove the active controller interleave mode.** No count is inferred from DIMM quantity, CPU maximum specifications or bandwidth.

**This machine** and result badges distinguish firmware layout, OS reports and controller detection. **Refresh memory topology** runs the built-in probe. A later annotation on matching GPU, CPU, motherboard, RAM capacity and reported clocks retains its capture time and marks historical inference conditions unverified; original sessions and inference rows stay unchanged. Pending configuration checks prompt when their benchmark's GPU is reconnected. Channel counts and provenance are included in helper CSV exports.

Helper throughput benchmarks run separate transfer microbenchmarks before inference by default. The API's `hardware_probe_policy: "defer"` skips fresh probes and reuses only a verified matching saved capture, or records that the measurement is deferred. Reused captures retain their original timestamp and are not presented as measured in the new session. Capability evaluations always use this separate-probe policy, keeping RAM, storage and CUDA microbenchmarks outside accuracy collection. **Measure transfer bandwidth** in the machine panel runs them independently. Choose **Storage test folder** on the drive holding your weights, or leave it blank to test the results volume; the folder path is excluded from saved public configuration. Storage → RAM reads a flushed 256 MiB temporary file three times in 8 MiB blocks at queue depth one, bypassing the OS page cache with Windows unbuffered I/O, Linux `O_DIRECT` or macOS `F_NOCACHE`. Device/controller caches may still contribute. File creation is excluded from read timing, and the temporary file is removed. This is sequential read throughput on the selected filesystem, not random expert-fetch performance or a measurement of other drives.

RAM → VRAM probes each detected NVIDIA adapter sequentially, mapped by PCI bus through the CUDA driver. Each device result retains its identity, raw samples and PCIe snapshots before and during untimed transfer warmup in `ram_to_vram_devices`. The selected primary adapter's result also appears in the compatibility field `ram_to_vram`; selecting it does not restrict the device sweep. The probe times completed copies from a 64 MiB pinned host buffer, with warmup, three 2 GiB samples, synchronization and a readback check. It describes host-to-device transfers, not internal VRAM bandwidth or pageable-memory performance. Separate device rates are not measured simultaneous throughput, and physical slot labels/wiring remain unverified. The probe avoids starting when reported free VRAM is below 512 MiB. Unsupported hardware, insufficient resources and failed probes are recorded as unavailable rather than estimated. No inference models are loaded or unloaded by the probes. An isolated worker has a 75-second limit.

`hardware.transfer_bandwidth` records protocol `wattever-transfer-v1`, capture time, scope, method, raw byte/time samples and their median bytes/second; UI rates use decimal MB/s and GB/s. Throughput execution sessions retain their own profile. Generic remote endpoints characterize the benchmark client, not the inference server. Browser-only mode cannot perform these native probes. A later measurement can be attached to a saved benchmark only on matching hardware and GPU/driver; it is marked `measured_later_on_matching_hardware`, with historical inference conditions unverified. Original inference measurements and session metadata are preserved.

Optional `reproducibility` settings and `performance_claims` are user-reported public annotations kept separate from detected fields. Record engine/version, model revision, quantization, context, KV precision and MTP draft count when known, plus placement and competing workloads in reviewed notes. Wattever does not invent TFLOPS from GPU names or model quantization. A sourced compute claim must state arithmetic precision, execution path, dense/sparse behavior and whether it is an advertised peak, independent measurement or estimate. Integer INT4/INT8 claims use TOPS; floating-point FP4/FP8/FP16/BF16/FP32 claims use TFLOP/s. Quantized weight storage does not establish inference arithmetic precision.

Quantization storage format (`quantization`, such as `Q4_0`) is separate from the method (`quantization_method`, such as QAT, QAD or UD). LM Studio discovery combines its model catalog and display labels, and records `quantization_source` and `quantization_method_source`. Unknown methods stay unknown; a four-bit format alone does not establish QAT or post-training quantization. Results and model selection show both labels when available. Historical catalog annotations use `lmstudio_catalog_backfill`, which does not verify historical weight bytes.

Each result can also carry a public `model_configuration` and `configuration_id`. It distinguishes requested model alias, canonical checkpoint, automatically resolved opaque endpoint ID/display name, operator reports and control-plane evidence. Endpoint naming provenance is detected, inferred, operator override or unknown; it is not established by ports or model aliases. The private URL-to-ID registry is excluded from public outputs, and URLs are not hashed into route IDs. Unknown quantization, reasoning or MTP is explicit. A configuration hash verifies consistency of public fields; it does not verify endpoint weights, effective settings or inference location. Historical user-reported endpoint identities remain readable. Capability task accuracy uses a separate protocol/result family; see [capability evaluation](docs/capabilities.md).

## Live telemetry and sustained observations

The helper samples whole-client CPU utilization and physical RAM usage independently of GPU sensor availability. The live dashboard shows combined GPU power/physical VRAM and a separate panel for each NVIDIA card. These measurements include competing processes and monitoring overhead; they do not isolate inference. Per-card VRAM percentage uses that adapter's capacity; combined occupancy uses summed used/capacity readings. CPU temperature is only ever an actual sensor reading, never an estimate. Linux may expose a CPU package sensor (hwmon `coretemp`, `k10temp` or `zenpower`). Windows has no unprivileged CPU package sensor. The System view offers an optional **Enable CPU temperature** button: after one administrator approval, it installs the signed [PawnIO](https://pawnio.eu/) driver (2.2.0, SHA-256 pinned) and a read-only Wattever task that reads only the CPU thermal registers (Intel `IA32_PACKAGE_THERM_STATUS`, AMD Tctl) and writes `%ProgramData%\Wattever\CpuSensor\cpu-temperature.json` every second (`cpu_temp_source` `windows_wattever_pawnio:intel_package` or `:amd_tctl`). **Remove CPU sensor** deletes the task and its files, and uninstalls PawnIO only if Wattever installed it. Without it, the helper reads a sensor tool that is already running: HWiNFO with Shared Memory Support enabled, or LibreHardwareMonitor with its web server on port 8085 (both report the CPU package, or Tctl/Tdie on AMD); otherwise Core Temp (the hottest core, labelled as such) or a live ACPI thermal zone (a firmware zone, not the CPU package, shown only once it has been seen to change because many boards report a fixed placeholder). `cpu_temp_source` names the source; when there is none, `cpu_temp_note` says why and the System view shows that reason. Missing temperatures remain null, including on macOS without an available temperature source.

RAM usage means physical total minus OS-reported available memory on Windows and Linux. macOS uses total minus free/inactive pages and labels that availability boundary as an estimate. CPU utilization uses host CPU-time deltas, not load average. GPU snapshots are held briefly while fresh; failed/stale sensors do not become zero utilization.

Stored `telemetry.history` contains elapsed seconds, UTC timestamps, scope and up to 3,600 recent points with explicit ring-retention counts. At 150 ms this covers roughly nine minutes; older points can be dropped. `telemetry.summary` preserves all-run observed sample means, time-weighted means, maxima, first/last readings and coverage despite history eviction. Raw phase samples retain up to 72,000 rows; a phase older than that retention is flagged incomplete.

All-card histories use scope `benchmark_client_all_nvidia_gpus`, with independent readings in each point's `gpus` array and per-card all-run statistics in `summary.gpus`. Single-query result `power.gpus` retains prefill/decode windows and energy per card; the existing scalar watt/joule fields now describe the declared combined boundary. Concurrent requests retain one whole-case `group_power` with per-card windows, avoiding overlapping energy double counting. The global VRAM peak is the peak of simultaneous sums, rather than the sum of independent card peaks. CSV exports include per-card columns and full per-card JSON. Covered all-run energy includes loading and idle; per-test energy is reported separately. Estimated CPU/system energy is always labeled as estimated.

Time-weighted coverage excludes long sampling gaps. Peaks are observed maxima and can miss shorter spikes. Early/late 60-second means can overlap on short runs. Changes in temperature, clocks or load describe the observed workload/environment; they do not establish throttling or prove sustained model throughput. Compare repeat throughput at matching workload and placement alongside thermal/load traces. Separate graphs per selected metric avoid sharing incompatible units on one chart.

## RAM and storage comparisons

Transfer profiles also measure native RAM copy payload throughput with one worker and several workers. Each worker uses disjoint 64 MiB source and destination buffers; committed pages, one warmup pass, three timed samples and readback checks are included. The working set exceeds typical CPU caches. Reported bytes count copied payload: logical source reads plus destination writes equal twice that count, while actual DRAM traffic depends on caching and write allocation. This is a copy microbenchmark, not peak DRAM bandwidth or a channel-count measurement.

In Machine details, use **Additional storage folders** to compare drives during the same measurement; separate existing folders with semicolons. Each volume gets its own temporary unbuffered read test and raw samples. The selected primary volume remains separate. Paths stay private; volume letters, available device model names and measured rates can be shared. Inference may benefit differently because model loading, mmap faults, OS caches and CPU/GPU overlap affect its I/O.

Execution sessions retain their hardware snapshot and transfer profile, including reported RAM clocks. Later independent captures remain available in **Independent hardware measurements**. This preserves conditions across storage or memory-setting experiments.

The collapsed **This machine** header shows CPU, GPU, RAM and per-card VRAM. Expanded Run and saved Results inventories use the same grouped compute/memory, storage, transfer and platform cards. Multiple GPUs keep separate memory capacities; unified memory is labeled shared. Full names, snapshot limitations and capture methods remain available in titles or disclosures.

After a helper restart, a compatible saved transfer capture can be displayed without running new probes or changing any benchmark. Its original timestamp and provenance remain intact, with **Saved capture** and `source: saved_capture`. Compatibility checks CPU/core counts, RAM capacity/modules, nonempty reported RAM clocks and all GPU names/memory/drivers. A clock or card change prevents reuse; independent captures take precedence over session captures.

Run and Results expose compact GPU, RAM/VRAM, storage and engine-setting badges. MTP badges distinguish requested, reported and verified states; unknown effective behavior stays unknown. Storage classes use reported media/bus evidence where available; an unspecified SATA device is not assumed to be an HDD. Full inventory and notes remain expandable. Bandwidth badges prefer an independent capture when available and identify it as **Independent probes**; hover for capture time and provenance. Each execution session retains its own probe measurements.

Results has three distinct views. **Overview** reports the system, coverage and, per model, peak prefill and decode speed, the change from the shortest to the longest completed prompt, the longest prompt completed with the first size that did not, and the change from the fewest to the most concurrent queries. Those trends are descriptive ratios of medians, not significance tests. **Graphs & comparisons** plots each ticked metric in its own chart, with all models together or one chart per model. **Tables & CSV** reports numerical medians and individual repeats. Graphs and tables share the metric, model and query-level toggles. Similar models are boxed together in the model list: first IDs that name the same model once the publisher, quantization and packaging are set aside ("4 variants"), then, among the rest, one family in several parameter counts ("4 sizes"). A box header shows or hides all of its models and **only** leaves just that box selected; a model with no sibling stays outside the boxes. The grouping reads names only and never changes what was measured. In Graphs, each benchmark in the chart key is a switch: click it to hide or show that benchmark's curves. Every ticked benchmark is on to begin with, an optional recorded condition such as an alternative storage run is offered switched off, and the notes above the charts count the passed tests that belong to switched-off benchmarks. A failed or skipped test that recorded fewer settings is filed under the measured condition it agrees with rather than shown as a separate condition; conditions are named as variants only when two of them measured the same model. A condition is defined by settings that can change a measured speed; where a label was reported from, a configuration hash that includes that provenance, and a session's test plan (sizes, repeats, selected cases) do not create one. Above the charts a banner counts the passed tests the current toggles draw. A test is counted as drawn when at least one ticked metric has a value for it; the rest are listed by cause (an unticked query count or prompt length, an unticked model, or a metric not recorded for that test) with a button for each remedy. Records made before request start offsets were kept have no whole-group prefill or decode rate above one query; those tests remain visible through per-request decode, time to first token, end-to-end output and completion time, and the affected charts say so. Recorded conditions retain visible checkboxes, selected/recorded totals and case/metric counts for the current selection. A condition with no matching model remains available as a choice but is omitted from that chart's legend.

Storage alternatives appear only when actual alternative inference rows are present. Installed drives or transfer probes do not imply a model was measured on them, and no storage type is required. **Compare recorded storage** selects the available primary/alternative conditions and experiment models, sets completion time, and opens Compare. SSD/NVMe observations retain separate identities, repeat medians, names and line styles. Default views retain primary observations. Median repeat values use the arithmetic middle for an even number of successes. Concurrent TTFT/prefill/decode metrics use per-query medians within each case; completion time covers all queries. For a single model, each chart includes the largest shared workload's exact values and repeat counts. Values use independent successful-repeat medians, matching the chart/table. Differences use matching successful repeats only; unequal subsets show the matched reference explicitly. Failure-only conditions remain in the legend/readout, and unpaired successes have no invented delta. Nearly overlapping curves can represent a measured small difference, as with IQ3_S in the recorded storage experiment.

**Table > All measurements** retains every selected repeat and exact query token counts/timings. Its **Export CSV** follows the selected conditions, models and query count. The Summary experiment's **Export both conditions CSV** exports the full frozen baseline and alternative, with per-query evidence in `request_metrics_json`. The helper's standard CSV API still exports primary measurements. Failed or unattempted cases never receive a paired speedup. See the [recorded 5060 Ti comparison](docs/5060-ti-storage-comparison.md) for actual values, both 80k repeats and cache/placement conditions.


## Automatic fallbacks and substitutions

Wattever continues a benchmark when a test cannot run as requested, or when a sensor or count is missing. Each of these behaviors is recorded with the result, so a row always says how it was actually measured. Compare rows only when these fields match.

### Placement fallback (managed LM Studio)

**Model placement** (`gpu_offload`) is the placement you request; the default is **Prefer GPU** (`max`). With **Use CPU memory if needed** (`fallback_on_failure`, on by default), a model that fails to load is loaded again with less of it on the GPU, in this order:

| Attempt | Placement | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | the requested placement, `max` by default | every layer on the GPU |
| 2 | `auto` | LM Studio chooses the placement |
| 3 | `0.5` | half of the layers on the GPU, the rest on the CPU |
| 4 | `off` | CPU only |

- The requested placement is not tried twice, and the ladder stops at the first load that succeeds. Each attempt is a complete load with its own load timeout (900 seconds by default).
- Every result records the placement that loaded in `gpu_offload`. Results shows it as **Placement** in **Table > All measurements** and in the CSV export, and chart notes name any placement other than `auto`.
- A result with `gpu_offload` `0.5` or `off` ran partly or wholly on the CPU. Its speed, power and memory describe that placement, so compare it only with rows that have the same `gpu_offload`. Loads that failed before the successful one appear in the helper log, not in the result.
- When every attempt fails, the test is recorded as failed with `fail_kind: "load_failed"`.
- Fallback loads can take much longer than the full-GPU tests around them: a large context that does not fit in VRAM usually runs very slowly on the CPU and can reach the per-test timeout. To measure GPU capacity only, turn **Use CPU memory if needed** off, or send `fallback_on_failure: false`. A load that does not fit is then recorded as a failure at the requested placement.
- External endpoints have no placement fallback. The inference engine controls placement, and results record `gpu_offload` as `externally_managed`.

### Other automatic behaviors

| Behavior | When it applies | What Wattever does | How the result records it | Control |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Skip larger sizes after a capacity failure | A model fails to load, overflows its context or exceeds the model's context limit | Records the larger prompt sizes for that model, technique and query count as skipped | `status: "skipped"`, `fail_kind: "skipped_after_failure"` | **Skip larger sizes after a capacity failure** (`stop_model_after_failure`, on by default) |
| Move on after a timeout | A test reaches the per-test timeout | Skips the remaining repeats and larger contexts for that model and query count | `status: "skipped"`, `fail_kind: "skipped_after_failure"`; the timed-out row keeps `fail_kind: "timeout"` | **Move on after a timeout** (`skip_after_timeout`, off by default) |
| MTP pass without an MTP head | MTP is requested for a model whose file has no supported MTP head | Skips that model's MTP pass and keeps its standard pass; the placement ladder is not used | `status: "skipped"`, `fail_kind: "mtp_unsupported"` | Choose **Off** for MTP |
| Context allocated by LM Studio | LM Studio rounds the requested context or limits it to the model's maximum | Runs the test with the context LM Studio allocated | `requested_total_context` (requested) and `context_length` (allocated) | Choose prompt sizes and query counts whose total fits the model's context limit |
| Power source | No NVIDIA sensor is readable | Uses `powermetrics` on macOS, otherwise records no GPU power | `power_source`: `nvidia-smi`, `powermetrics` or `none`; `system_w_est` is always an estimate | None |
| CPU temperature source | No CPU package sensor is readable | On Windows, reads the optional Wattever PawnIO sensor, then HWiNFO, then LibreHardwareMonitor, then Core Temp, then a live ACPI thermal zone; otherwise reports no value | `cpu_temp_source` names the sensor; `cpu_temp_note` says why a value is missing | **Enable CPU temperature** in System, or run one of the sensor tools |
| Output token count | The provider's stream carries no token usage | Leaves throughput unavailable instead of counting stream chunks | `metric_sources.completion_tokens`: `server_usage` or `unavailable`; an estimated count sets `completion_tokens_estimated` | Use a provider that reports usage |
| Endpoint name | An endpoint exposes no recognized service metadata | Names it Local, Private or Remote endpoint | The endpoint label | Set the optional **Display name override** |

See [troubleshooting](docs/troubleshooting.md) for the matching symptoms and [API](docs/api.md) for the request fields.

## Sessions and recovery

Each benchmark has one JSON file in `results/runs/`. The local helper supports same-file additions and repairs for both LM Studio and external endpoints. Reconnect the original external endpoint before repairing its tests; URLs and credentials are not saved. A timeout stops the generic run because Wattever cannot verify provider-side cancellation or unload. Inspect the engine before continuing.

Other failed requests on an external endpoint do not stop the run. The helper sends one short request to the same model. If the model answers, only that test failed and the benchmark goes on. If the endpoint answers but refuses the model, the test is recorded with `fail_kind: "model_unavailable"`, the model's remaining tests are recorded as skipped and the next model starts. If the endpoint does not answer within a minute, rejects the API key, or the check itself times out, the run stops with an explanation and the tests that never ran stay unrecorded, so the benchmark can be continued later. The test in flight when an endpoint disappeared is kept as a failure (`endpoint_unreachable`); include it with **Retry failed tests**. Each such row carries `endpoint_check` with the verdict and the HTTP status that decided it.

In Results, choose **Add / rerun tests**. Select an installed or served model to add it to the existing GPU benchmark, then review the workload and test counts. LM Studio offers Standard/MTP modes; external MTP stays provider controlled. Select one visible model and choose **Rerun selected model** to repeat its workload. Increase **Total repeats per test** to append repeat slots without replacing saved measurements. Set **Timeout per test** for new attempts, including individual repairs; each session and result retains its actual budget. In **Tests to update**, choose one saved model/size/query-count/repeat to repair only that test; the All measurements table also provides a **Repair repeat** button. **Add missing tests** preserves terminal cases; **Retry failed tests** includes failures and skips; **Rerun selected tests** includes successful cases. A replaced attempt moves to `previous_attempts` and is not averaged with its replacement. An exact snapshot is kept in `results/.history/`. Each execution has session settings, hardware inventory, measurement scope and provenance. Mixed benchmarks retain control and hardware attribution separately for each engine. Resume creates a new run for unfinished work. Additions and repairs require compatible hardware, selected GPU/driver and corpus. Managed tests also require the saved LM Studio version; external repairs require the saved endpoint identity. Otherwise start a new benchmark. External model loading remains under the engine operator's control.

To remove a model, select one benchmark and show only that model in the Models filter, then choose **Remove selected model** and confirm. Its measurements and planned workloads are removed; other models stay in place. A history backup preserves the original file. For the last model, use **Delete benchmark**. Shared community entries are read-only; these editing controls apply to the local helper's saved benchmarks.

Managed requests receive the configured per-test timeout. Prefill speed at shorter contexts does not shorten the budget for a larger context. The same whole-test budget applies while waiting for first output and during decode; output pauses do not impose a shorter hidden deadline. A timeout is a time limit, not physical freeze detection. The helper verifies managed model unload and worker exit before continuing; if verification fails, the run stops. Capacity failures can skip larger cases for that model/concurrency. By default, timeouts and transient request errors do not suppress subsequent repeats or larger contexts; a timed-out managed model is reloaded before another repeat. In the extension dialog's **Failure policy**, you can disable CPU placement fallback and opt to skip remaining repeats and larger contexts after a timeout. This records a practical time limit and explicit skips; it does not establish a hard VRAM allocation limit.

Older schemas and planner settings remain readable. An extended legacy run can contain sessions with different context planning; compare session settings rather than treating them as identical. See [API](docs/api.md), [FAQ](docs/faq.md), and [results guidance](results/README.md).

---

## docs/capabilities.md

Canonical source: [docs/capabilities.md](docs/capabilities.md)

# Capability evaluation

New question subsets use versioned SHA256 ranking of the selection seed and stable item IDs, independent of Python's sampling implementation. Historical Python-sampling records remain readable. Each run also records the exact selected IDs and their digest.

Use **Capabilities** to compare rule-scored task accuracy separately from throughput and power. Connect an endpoint in **Benchmarks**, then choose a model, suite, question count, seed, repeats and generation budget. Its display name and opaque route identity are supplied automatically. Launching tests and validating capability imports require the local Python helper. The hosted site can browse, export and compare shared capability results; it does not launch capability inference or import unvalidated capability files.

## Bundled suites

| Suite ID | Questions | Evaluation |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| `wattever-core-v1` | 24 | Original arithmetic, logic, typed JSON, instruction, retrieval and code-output tasks; four per category |
| `gsm8k-test-chat-v1` | 1,319 | GSM8K test split; zero-shot chat with final numeric-answer matching |
| `arc-challenge-test-chat-v1` | 1,172 | ARC-Challenge test split; zero-shot chat with generated answer-letter matching |
| `mmlu-pro-test-chat-v1` | 12,032 | MMLU-Pro test split, 14 subjects and up to ten choices; zero-shot generated letters |
| `mmlu-pro-balanced64-chat-v1` | 64 | Fixed category-balanced MMLU-Pro subset, four or five questions per subject; zero-shot generated letters |

The external test splits are bundled for offline use. GSM8K is pinned to upstream revision `3101c7d5072418e28b9008a6636bde82a006892c` under MIT. ARC uses the `ARC-V1-Feb2018` archive's Challenge test member under CC BY-SA 4.0. The loader checks each extracted file's exact SHA-256 and item count before registering a suite. Source links, hashes, archive member, attribution and licenses are in [dataset provenance](corpora/capabilities/README.md). The archive ETag records source provenance; it is not the extracted file's cryptographic checksum.

MMLU-Pro is pinned to dataset revision `b189ec765aa7ed75c8acfea42df31fdae71f97be`, whose dataset card declares MIT. Its bundled JSONL preserves question text, options, keys and subjects while excluding gold chain-of-thought explanations. The separate balanced 64 suite selects questions by stable ID and subject using seed `73129`; no answer or model result determines selection. It defaults to **Full suite**, which tests all 64 questions. Its subject weighting differs from the full 12,032-question test split. Subsampling that 64-question suite again does not preserve its guaranteed four-to-five questions per subject.

The Capabilities interface initially selects the balanced 64-question suite when it is available, and preserves an available selection on refresh. The API has separate defaults; see [API configuration](docs/api.md).

Both MMLU-Pro suites use zero-shot chat and generated final answer letters. They are separate from the official five-shot chain-of-thought protocol and its leaderboard scores. Full suites can be expensive: imports and suite registration allow at most 20,000 questions, with existing limits of 200,000 characters per prompt and 20 million total prompt characters.

**AI2 ARC-Challenge** contains grade-school multiple-choice science questions. It is distinct from the [ARC-AGI grid-reasoning benchmark](https://arcprize.org/arc-agi/1). The dashboard identifies its task type explicitly. A high score on this science-question suite is not an ARC-AGI score or a general intelligence rating. See the [AI2 dataset description](https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/ai2_arc).

These are versioned Wattever chat adaptations. GSM8K uses a zero-shot final `#### <number>` answer rather than a published few-shot harness. ARC normalizes option labels to letters and grades generated `ANSWER: <letter>` output rather than option likelihoods. Different prompts, sampling, item selections, output budgets and graders can change results. Do not equate these scores with official leaderboard or other harness scores. Public tasks may have appeared in training; none of these suites measures IQ or establishes a general intelligence ranking. Core is a small functional probe with a possible ceiling effect. For a more demanding comparison, choose MMLU-Pro or another relevant published suite and inspect the exact questions and coverage; difficulty alone does not validate a score as a measure of general intelligence.

## Run and compare

1. Start the inference engine and load the intended model. Connect it in **Benchmarks**; no manual endpoint ID or label is needed. Use an optional canonical model ID if its served alias is ambiguous. An advanced **Display name** override can clarify an ambiguous detected name; keep it public and free of connection URLs or credentials.
2. Record quantization, model revision, engine/version, context/KV settings, reported reasoning and MTP where known. Configure actual settings in the engine. An omitted or unknown field does not mean disabled.
3. Open **Capabilities**, select the model and suite, and choose a subset or **Full suite**. The seed selects a deterministic subset; its exact IDs and digest are recorded. Use the same selection and evaluation settings across comparisons. Full suites can take substantial time and provider usage.
4. Review total generation tokens, optional deadline and repeats. Capability generation settings are independent of the speed benchmark. The default budget is 32,768 tokens for thinking plus final output, with no wall-clock deadline (`0`). This is a ceiling, not a request to generate that many tokens. The server's loaded context and provider limits can impose lower limits. Use Stop to cancel, or set an explicit item deadline when needed. The UI defaults requested reasoning to **None**; **Provider default** omits that API field. Unsupported reasoning requests fail visibly. A short total budget can truncate reasoning before a final answer appears. Inspect the observed reasoning, token usage, output-limit count and coverage; a requested reasoning setting does not prove the engine honored it. Keep budgets consistent across comparable configurations and report deliberate budget changes as separate evaluations.
5. Start the test. One request runs at a time, with a fresh chat per item/repeat. No model load/unload or MTP command is sent. Local CPU/RAM/GPU telemetry is available only after explicitly confirming inference runs on this computer, including when using an LM Studio endpoint.
6. Open a saved result to explore its dashboard. Select category bars, outcomes or repeats to filter the question matrix, then select a cell to inspect the prompt, expected output and visible response. Select multiple results for configuration comparisons. Different evaluation keys indicate different experiments.

Requested sampling is recorded, including temperature, optional top-p and reasoning effort.
